threads.thread_goal: Align on overall seasonal theme, bundles, and campaign calendar.

messages.text: Kicking off the seasonal promo planning for Cross-Department Seasonal Promotions for Food and Garden Retail. I have a first draft for the overall theme and calendar in A1, based on T1 and some ideas for T4. Proposal: theme 'Spring Table and Garden Days' for the 3-week window. Week 1: focus on bakery breakfasts and light lunches. Week 2: grill and roast focus from meat, with bakery sides. Week 3: leftovers and waste reduction ideas, plus garden corner for outdoor meals. Bundles draft: 1) Lunch combo: restaurant soup or salad + bakery bread + meat cold cuts. 2) Weekend roast: meat roast cut + bakery dessert suggestion + potted herbs from garden. 3) Coffee and cake: bakery slice + coffee, with a flyer pointing to garden gifts. Before we lock anything, I would like your feedback on whether this feels realistic for your sections and stock.

Thanks for sharing the draft. From meat side, the 3-week split makes sense, especially a strong grill and roast focus in week 2. For T4, if the restaurant menu uses more roast and grill cuts, we can align our bundles in T1 so we push the same items. One concern: if we push roasts too hard in week 2, we might overstock and hit the waste risk mentioned in the project. I suggest we keep week 1 as a soft ramp-up for meat, with more cold cuts and marinated items that can roll into week 2 if needed. Also, for the weekend roast bundle, we should define 2 or 3 specific cuts with clear price points so signage is simple.

From my side in meat, I like the grill and roast idea. For the bundles, maybe we can add a simple weekday option: small pack of marinated meat + bakery roll pack, so people can do quick dinners. That could fit in week 1 and 2. For week 3, maybe we can promote sliced leftover roast for sandwiches with bakery bread, to help with waste. I am not sure how to fit garden items into that last week though, maybe @43478 can suggest plants that match the leftover theme.

On the garden side, 'Spring Table and Garden Days' works well for T1. For week 1, I can highlight small table plants and simple flower arrangements that people can take home with bakery breakfast or coffee. Week 2, we can push herbs and maybe some outdoor plants that go with grilling. Week 3, I could show easy-care plants and maybe compost-friendly info to connect with the waste reduction focus. For bundles, I can add a small sign near herbs saying something like: 'Pair these herbs with your roast from meat and fresh bread from bakery'. I will need help later to make sure the wording fits T4 and the restaurant menu.

Agree that the theme sounds good and easy to explain to customers. For the weekend roast bundle, we should also think about how it shows up in the restaurant. Maybe a weekend plate that uses the same cut we promote in the counter, so staff can point customers both ways. That would help T4 and keep stock rotation under control. On the calendar, I would suggest we mark specific 'grill days' in A1, maybe Fridays and Saturdays in week 2, so we can plan staffing and sampling better.

Good points on the waste risk. To keep it manageable, I can adjust A1 so week 1 has a light meat focus: cold cuts and marinated items that can roll into week 2, as you suggested. For T4, I will draft 3 restaurant dishes: 1) grilled plate using the same cuts as the weekend roast bundle, 2) lunch salad with cold cuts and bakery bread, 3) leftover roast sandwich for week 3. I will also mark 'grill days' on Fridays and Saturdays in the calendar. Before I update A1, can we agree that 'Spring Table and Garden Days' is our main theme, or do you see any better wording?

From my side, 'Spring Table and Garden Days' works. It connects food and plants clearly and is easy to put on signage and in scripts. I suggest we keep the three main cross-section bundles you listed, but refine them slightly: 1) Lunch combo: restaurant salad or soup + bakery bread + meat cold cuts. 2) Weekend roast: specific roast cut + bakery dessert suggestion + potted herbs. 3) Coffee and cake: bakery slice + coffee, with a small garden gift suggestion. If everyone is ok, we can treat these as the main bundles for T1 and reflect them in A1.

I am fine with 'Spring Table and Garden Days' as the theme. The three bundles are clear enough for me to explain to customers. For the garden part, I will make sure we always have herbs ready for the weekend roast bundle and some small plants near the coffee and cake area. I will need help later to make sure the exact plant names and prices fit the budget, but conceptually I am aligned.

Agree with the theme and the three bundles. For the weekday marinated meat + bakery rolls idea I mentioned, we can treat that as a sub-offer under the lunch combo, so we do not overload A1 with too many main bundles. I will coordinate with bakery on which rolls to highlight so we keep it simple.

Same here, I am aligned with the theme and bundles. For the weekend roast bundle, I suggest we pick: pork shoulder, chicken legs, and one beef option, each with a clear price and limit per customer. That will help later when we work on T10 and signage. We can detail that in the meat thread, but I wanted to flag it now so it is considered in A1.

Ok, sounds like we are aligned on 'Spring Table and Garden Days' and the three main bundles. I will update A1 and T1 to reflect: 1) Lunch combo, 2) Weekend roast, 3) Coffee and cake, plus the weekday marinated meat + rolls as a sub-offer. Next, we need to be precise on the 3-week calendar and key focus days. Proposal: Week 1: soft launch, focus on lunch combo and coffee and cake, with garden table plants. Week 2: strong grill and roast focus, with grill days on Friday and Saturday, plus herbs. Week 3: leftover roast sandwich in restaurant, bakery bread for sandwiches, and easy-care plants. Does this calendar work with your staffing and stock routines, or do we need to shift any focus days?

Calendar looks workable. Only adjustment I would suggest is to start signaling the grill focus already on the first Friday of week 1, maybe as a teaser with smaller quantities. That way we can test demand before the full push in week 2 and reduce the risk of overstock. For week 3, we should make sure the leftover roast sandwich in T4 is clearly tied to any meat we still have, so we can adjust daily based on stock.

From garden side, the calendar is fine. I just need the exact dates for the grill days and the leftover week so I can plan which plants to order and when to display them. For example, herbs should be freshest in week 2, and easy-care plants can be more visible in week 3. If you add those dates into A1, I can follow them.

The calendar works for me. The only thing I would add is a note in A1 that on Mondays we review what sold over the weekend and adjust orders for meat and bakery-linked items. That will help with the waste risk and keep T4 aligned with what we actually have.
Agree with the calendar and with adding a small grill teaser on the first Friday. That will also help us test the display flow before the main push. No other changes from my side.

Got it. I will update A1 so that: 1) Week 1 includes a small grill teaser on the first Friday, 2) Week 2 has full grill and roast focus with grill days on Friday and Saturday, 3) Week 3 is clearly marked as leftover and waste reduction focus, with the sandwich offer from T4. I will also add a Monday review note to adjust orders and menu items based on sales and stock. With these changes, can we say the 3-week promotion calendar and key focus days are approved so I can close T1 and move on to detailing T4 with finance?

From meat side, yes, I am ok to approve the 3-week calendar and focus days as you described. The Monday review and grill teaser are good safeguards. Once A1 is updated, we can use it as the reference for our detailed meat bundles and displays.
I am also ok with the calendar and focus days. Once you share the updated A1, I will use it to plan the garden corner for T5 so that plants and herbs match each week.
Ok for me as well. The Monday review note will help us react if any bundle underperforms. I will watch the first grill teaser Friday and share feedback so we can tweak week 2 if needed.
Aligned from my side too. With the calendar approved, we can start preparing the meat and bakery-linked offers and make sure our staff know which days to push which bundle.

Thanks all. I will update A1 today with the final theme, bundles, and calendar, and mark T1 as ready. Then I will start drafting the three restaurant dishes for T4 and check costs with finance so we stay within the budget constraint.

threads.thread_goal: Define and agree on display layouts for bakery, meat, and garden corners.

messages.text: Starting the display layout discussion for bakery and meat stands, plus how we link to the garden corner. I have sketched a first version for T2 and T10 and added notes into A5. Proposal for meat: 1) Main grill and roast table near the meat counter, with three clear zones: grill cuts, roast cuts, and marinated weekday packs. 2) Signage strip on top with the 'Spring Table and Garden Days' theme and icons for bakery and garden. 3) Small side shelf with recipe cards pointing to restaurant dishes from T4. For bakery, I suggest a facing stand near the meat area with bread and dessert items that match the bundles. For T9, we can use the front of that stand for sampling on key days. For the garden corner, I imagine a visual link using herbs and small plants placed between the meat and bakery stands, but I need @43478 to confirm what is realistic. Feedback welcome before we lock anything in A5.

I like the three-zone idea for the meat table. It will help us guide customers quickly. For T2, maybe we should keep the marinated weekday packs closer to the front, since they are easier to explain and can move faster. For T9, if we use the bakery stand front for sampling, we need to make sure there is enough space for plates and that hygiene rules are clear. Maybe we can add a small tray area in the sketch in A5.

Agree with the overall layout. One thing to watch is the cold chain and display time limits for T10. The grill and roast cuts should stay closest to the refrigerated area, and we should not overload the table with product that cannot be kept at the right temperature. Maybe we can use more dummy packs or empty boxes to build height and keep real product in the chilled area.

From restaurant side, I like the idea of recipe cards linking to T4 dishes. We just need to keep them simple: one card per dish, with a photo, short description, and a note on which meat cut and bakery item it uses. For the bakery stand, we should also think about how customers flow between meat, bakery, and garden. If the bakery stand is too close to the meat counter, we might create a bottleneck during peak hours.

For the garden link, I can prepare a small herb and plant display that sits between the meat and bakery stands, as you suggested. For T5, I imagine a low table with potted herbs and a few small flower arrangements, plus a sign that repeats the 'Spring Table and Garden Days' theme. I will need to know the exact space we have so I do not block the aisle. Maybe we can mark it on the A5 sketch.

Good call on the marinated packs. I will adjust the A5 sketch so the front zone is 'Quick weekday dinners' with marinated packs and matching bakery rolls, then 'Weekend grill' and 'Roast' zones behind. For T9, I will add a dedicated sampling shelf on the bakery stand front, with space for trays and tongs, and a small sign reminding staff about hygiene steps. We will detail the hygiene and handling in T9, but at least the layout will support it.

On cold chain and T10, fully agree. In the updated A5, I will keep the real product only in the chilled area and use empty boxes or dummy packs to build the visual pyramid on the table. We will also add a note that any product placed on the table must respect display time limits and be rotated back if not sold. I will need the exact time limits from our food safety rules, so I will check with the store manager before we finalize T10.

On the bakery stand bottleneck, maybe we can angle the stand slightly so customers can see the bread and desserts from the main aisle without having to stand right in front of the meat counter. That way, people waiting for meat can still see the bakery items, but others can pass by. We can draw that angle into A5.

For space, we need to keep a clear path for trolleys. I suggest the herb and plant table for T5 is no deeper than half a standard pallet and sits slightly offset from the main aisle. If you add that dimension into A6 and we reflect it in A5, we should be safe. Also, can we make sure the garden display has at least one sign that points back to the meat and bakery bundles, so customers understand the link?

Yes, I can keep the table shallow and offset as you described. In A6, I will note the half-pallet depth and add a sign that says something like: 'Complete your spring table: pick your roast from meat and bread from bakery, then add fresh herbs here'. I will share a quick sketch so you can see if it fits T5.

Angling the bakery stand sounds good. We should also keep the top of the stand low enough so customers can still see the meat counter staff. That helps with service and reduces confusion. Maybe we can limit the height of the back shelf in A5.

I will incorporate the angled bakery stand and lower back shelf into the A5 sketch. So summarizing the current layout for T2 and T10: 1) Meat table with three zones, real product only in chilled area, dummy packs for height. 2) Bakery stand angled to the aisle, with front sampling shelf for T9 and limited height. 3) Herb and plant table between them, shallow and offset, as per A6. If everyone is ok with this concept, we can treat it as the base layout and only fine-tune details later.

From my side, that summary works. The only addition I would ask is a small space on the meat table or nearby for a stand with the restaurant menu specials from T4, so staff can point to it when explaining the bundles. It does not need to be big, just visible.

I am ok with the base layout. The three zones and angled bakery stand will make it easier to talk customers through the offers. For T9, we just need to remember to keep the sampling area close to the bakery staff so they can watch it and keep it tidy.

I am also fine with the base layout. The herb and plant table between meat and bakery will make it easy for me to explain the connection to customers. I will make sure A6 reflects the final position and that the signs mention both food sections.

Good point. I will add a small menu stand area into A5, next to the meat table but not blocking the flow. That stand will hold the specials from T4 and any flyers we create. With that addition, can we say the display layout guidelines for bakery and meat stands in T2 are approved, so I can finalize A5 and move on to detailing T9 and T10?
Yes, from my side the bakery and meat layouts are good to go as described in A5. The menu stand addition is useful and should not create extra clutter if we keep it small.
Agreed, the layouts are clear enough for us to implement. We can fine-tune small things on site, but the structure in A5 is solid.
I am ok to approve the bakery and meat display guidelines as captured in A5. This will help keep execution consistent across shifts.

On the garden corner, with the herb and plant table between meat and bakery, plus the sign text you suggested in A6, I think the visual link to the food theme is clear. We will just need to make sure the colors and fonts match the main theme from A1 so customers see it as one campaign.

I can align the colors and fonts in A6 with what you have in A1. So the garden corner will show herbs and small plants between meat and bakery, with signs that mention both sections and the 'Spring Table and Garden Days' theme. If everyone agrees, we can treat this as the final way the garden corner links visually to the food theme for T5.

From my side, that works well. The herb and plant table between the stands, with matching theme visuals, makes the connection very obvious for customers. I am ok to confirm this as the visual link for T5.
Agreed, the garden corner plan in A6 clearly ties into the food theme and bundles. We can go ahead with that setup for T5.
Great, I will finalize A5 today with the approved layouts and then start drafting the detailed sampling plan for T9 and the bundle and storage notes for T10.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize cross-selling scripts, signage wording, and legal info.

messages.text: I have a first draft of cross-selling scripts and sign texts for T3 and T11, captured in A2. These are short phrases we can all use. Examples: 1) For lunch combo: 'If you are choosing soup or salad today, we have fresh bread from bakery and sliced cold cuts from meat that match our Spring Table and Garden Days offer.' 2) For weekend roast: 'Planning a roast this weekend? You can pick your cut here, then grab dessert from bakery and fresh herbs from the garden corner just next to us.' 3) For coffee and cake: 'With your coffee and cake, you can also pick a small plant from our garden corner as a simple gift.' For signage, I drafted simple wording in T11 like 'Spring Table and Garden Days: Mix and match meat, bakery, and garden for your perfect meal.' I am less sure about the legal and pricing info we must add, so I will need help from you and the manager to check that part.

Thanks for putting this together. The scripts are clear and match the theme in A1. For T3, we should probably add at least two more scenarios: one for customers who start in the garden corner and one for those who are mainly in the restaurant. Also, for T11, we must make sure the signs show prices clearly and include any mandatory food and allergen information. I can check the legal wording with the store manager, but I will need your draft texts in a simple list format.

The tone of the scripts works well for the meat counter. For T3, I suggest we add a very short version we can use when it is busy, something like: 'We have a spring combo with bread from bakery and herbs from the garden corner if you like.' That way we can still mention the cross-sell without slowing down the line. On signage for T11, we should avoid any wording that sounds like a fixed bundle price unless we actually have a clear price printed, to stay safe on pricing rules.

I like the examples. For the weekend roast script, maybe we can be more concrete: 'Planning a roast this weekend? This pork shoulder is on our Spring Table and Garden Days offer. You can add dessert from bakery and fresh herbs from the garden corner.' That way we point to a specific cut and make it easier for customers to decide.

For the garden-start scenario, maybe something like: 'If you are choosing herbs or plants for your table, we also have matching bread in bakery and roast cuts in meat as part of our Spring Table and Garden Days.' That could go into A2 as one of the five required scenarios for T3.

Ok, I will expand A2 with: 1) a garden-start script like the one suggested, 2) a restaurant-start script, and 3) a short busy-time version for meat and bakery. That should give us at least five scenarios for T3. For T11, I will rewrite the sign texts into a simple list and leave space for price and legal info, then you can check with the store manager.

Great. For the restaurant-start script, we can say something like: 'If you enjoyed this dish, you can find the same roast cut in the meat section and matching bread in bakery as part of our Spring Table and Garden Days.' Please add that to A2. Once you have the list of sign texts for T11, I will review them and then check the legal parts with the store manager.

On the signage wording for T11, I suggest we keep the main headline as 'Spring Table and Garden Days' and then have sub-lines like 'Pick your roast cut here' or 'Add fresh herbs from the garden corner'. Prices should be clearly listed next to each product, not hidden in the text. That will make it easier to stay compliant when prices change.

Agree. Also, for T10 we will have some limits on how long certain cuts can stay on display. Maybe we should avoid promising that a specific cut is always available in the scripts. Instead, we can say 'today we have' and then name the cut, so staff can adapt if stock changes.

Good point. I will adjust the scripts in A2 to use 'today we have' instead of promising a fixed cut, so staff can adapt to stock and T10 constraints. For the signs in T11, I will avoid naming specific cuts in the main text and leave that to the price labels.

Once you update A2 and T11 with these changes, please ping here. I will then review the scripts and sign texts and check the legal and pricing parts with the store manager. After that, we should be ready to approve the final scripts for T3 and the wording for T11.

I have now updated A2 with five scenarios: 1) lunch combo, 2) weekend roast, 3) coffee and cake, 4) garden-start, 5) restaurant-start, plus a short busy-time version. I also rewrote the sign texts in T11 as a list: main headline, sub-lines for each section, and placeholders for prices and legal info. Please review and let me know if anything is unclear.

I went through A2. The scripts are short and practical. From meat side, I am comfortable using them as they are now, including the busy-time version. They cover the main situations we see at the counter.
Same here, the updated scripts in A2 look good. I like that they are flexible with 'today we have', so we can adapt to stock. No further changes from my side.

I have reviewed A2 and the sign texts in T11. I also checked the legal and pricing parts with the store manager. We will need to add allergen icons on the restaurant and bakery signs and make sure all prices are clearly visible next to the products, but the wording itself is fine. With those icons and price labels added, I am ok to approve the cross-selling scripts in A2 for T3.
Good to hear the store manager is ok with the wording. With the allergen icons and clear prices added, I am comfortable saying the scripts in A2 are final for T3.
Agreed, the scripts are ready to use. They will help us keep the message consistent across shifts.

On the signage wording in T11, with the headline, sub-lines per section, allergen icons, and clear prices next to each product, the store manager confirmed we are compliant. So I am ok to approve the final wording and mandatory information for signage as described in T11.
Ok, I will treat the scripts in A2 and the sign texts in T11 as final. I will prepare the final version of A2 for printing and share it in the channel so everyone can access it easily.

threads.thread_goal: Set up waste control, stock rotation, and tracking routines.

messages.text: I have drafted a food waste and stock rotation checklist for T6 and a simple sales and waste tracking sheet for T7, captured in A3 and A4. The checklist covers bakery, meat, and restaurant stock points, with daily checks for: 1) date and time, 2) stock rotation done, 3) markdowns applied, 4) items moved between sections if possible. The tracking sheet A4 has columns for each day, per section: sales, waste, and notes. Proposal for responsibilities: meat team fills meat lines, bakery team fills bakery lines, and I fill restaurant lines and consolidate. Before we confirm, I want to check if this is realistic for your shifts and if we need to simplify anything.

Thanks for setting this up. The structure of A3 and A4 looks workable. For T6, I suggest we assign specific times for the checks: for meat, a quick check at opening and another before the evening rush. That way it becomes part of the routine. For T7, we should define who fills the sheet on days when the usual person is off, so we do not miss data.

From my side, I can take the meat checklist at opening, but I might not always be there before the evening rush. Maybe we can say: opening check by whoever opens meat, and pre-evening check by whoever is closing. For A4, I am ok to fill the meat sales and waste lines, but I will need a quick explanation on how to estimate waste correctly, especially for trimmed meat.

I agree with the idea of splitting responsibilities by section. For bakery, we should probably do the checklist after the morning bake and again late afternoon, since that is when we see most waste risk. On A4, maybe we can keep the notes column simple, just a few standard codes like 'promo', 'weather', or 'staffing', so we do not spend too much time writing.

For the garden corner, I do not have food waste, but I can still use A3 to check plant freshness and markdowns. I can fill a simple line in A4 for garden sales and any plants we have to discard, so we see the full picture of the promotion.

Ok, I will update A3 so that: 1) meat checks are at opening and before evening rush, 2) bakery checks are after morning bake and late afternoon, 3) restaurant checks are before lunch and before dinner. For A4, I like the idea of standard codes in the notes column. I will add a small legend at the top. On backup responsibilities, we can say: if the usual person is off, the shift lead for that section fills the sheet.

For estimating waste in meat, we can keep it simple: count or weigh the product that is no longer sellable and record that. For trimmed meat that is still usable, we should not count it as waste if we can rework it into another product. Maybe we can add a short note in A3 explaining this, so everyone does it the same way.

Good suggestion. I will add a short note in A3 about how to count waste vs rework, and we can also cover this in the mini-training for T8. For A4, I will keep the garden line you suggested, so we can see if plant markdowns are linked to the promotion timing.
That explanation helps. With a clear note in A3, I am comfortable filling the meat waste lines in A4. I just need to see the final version once you update it.

The timing you proposed for bakery checks works for me. For A4, the standard codes will save time. Maybe we can also add a code for 'stock issue' when we get short deliveries, so we can explain low sales that are not due to demand.

I will add a 'stock issue' code to the legend in A4. So, to summarize responsibilities: 1) Meat team: opening and pre-evening checks in A3 for meat, fill meat lines in A4 daily. 2) Bakery team: post-bake and late afternoon checks in A3 for bakery, fill bakery lines in A4. 3) Restaurant: pre-lunch and pre-dinner checks in A3, fill restaurant lines in A4 and consolidate. 4) Garden: daily freshness and markdown check in A3, fill garden line in A4. Backup: shift lead fills if the usual person is off. Does this division work for everyone?
From meat side, that division is clear and manageable. I am ok to confirm that we will own the meat checklist and tracking entries as described.
Works for me too. With the clear times and notes in A3, it should be easy to remember.
I am ok with the bakery responsibilities as you described. We will make sure the late afternoon check is done even on busy days.
I can handle the garden checks and A4 line as you described. It will also help me see which plants move better during the promotion.

Great, thanks all. With this division confirmed, I will finalize A3 and A4 and add a test entry for the first day in A4 as required by T7. We can then treat these routines as agreed for the promotion period.

threads.thread_goal: Plan launch mini-training and define success review approach.

messages.text: We are close to launch, so I drafted a mini-training agenda for T8 and a simple review plan for T12, captured in A7 and A8. Proposal for the launch huddle (30 minutes): 1) 10 min: overview of theme and bundles from A1. 2) 10 min: quick run-through of scripts from A2 and key signage points from T11. 3) 10 min: displays and routines, including A5, A6, A3, and A4. I suggest we run two sessions on launch day: one before opening and one mid-afternoon, so all shifts can attend. For the end-of-campaign review in A8 and T12, I propose we look at A4 data, list what worked and what did not, and capture 3 improvement ideas. Does this timing and content work for you, or do we need to adjust?

The agenda in A7 covers the right topics. For meat, a pre-opening session works well, but a mid-afternoon one might clash with our prep for the evening rush. Could we do the second session slightly earlier, maybe just after lunch, so we are not pulled away at a critical time?

Content looks good. I would appreciate a quick practical demo during the training: for example, one of us walks through the meat and bakery displays and uses one of the scripts from A2 with a mock customer. That will make it easier to remember than just reading.

Agree on the need for a demo. Also, maybe we can keep the part on A3 and A4 very concrete: show one filled example line for each section, so people see exactly what is expected. That should help avoid confusion later when we collect data for A8 and T12.

For garden, the proposed times are ok as long as we know them a bit in advance so I can plan watering and deliveries around them. In the training, I would like a short moment to explain the garden corner plan from A6 and how I will talk about the bundles, so others know what I am saying to customers.

Ok, we can move the second session earlier. Proposal: first session 30 minutes before opening, second session at 14:30. That should avoid the evening rush and still catch most afternoon staff. I will update A7 with these times and add a short live demo segment using A2 and the displays from A5 and A6, as suggested.

Those times work better for meat. During the demo, I can volunteer to play the staff role at the meat counter and walk through one or two scripts from A2, so others see how to keep it short when it is busy.
14:30 works for me. Showing one filled example line in A4 for each section is a good idea. Maybe we can prepare those examples in advance so we do not improvise during the session.
I can help prepare the bakery example line in A4 before the training. That way we have at least one realistic case to show.
14:30 is fine for me too. During the training, I can quickly show the herb and plant table from A6 and say the main script I will use, so others hear it once.

On the review plan in A8 and T12, I propose we schedule a 30-minute session in the week after the promotion ends. Agenda: 1) look at A4 totals per section, 2) each section shares one success and one issue, 3) we agree on three concrete improvements for next time. I will prepare a simple slide or printout from A4 to make it easier to see the numbers.
That review format works for me. It is focused and should not take too long. Maybe we can also note any display changes that worked well, so we remember them for the next seasonal campaign.

I like the idea of each section bringing one success and one issue. That will keep the discussion concrete. We just need to make sure A4 is fully filled before the review, otherwise we will be guessing.
Agreed. For bakery, I can prepare a quick note on which upsell offers from T9 worked best, so we can link the numbers in A4 to specific actions.
For garden, I will bring which plants sold best and which ones we had to mark down, so we can adjust the selection next time. I will base it on my line in A4.

Ok, so summarizing T8: 1) Two sessions on launch day, 30 minutes each, at pre-opening and 14:30. 2) Agenda in A7: theme and bundles from A1, scripts from A2 and signage from T11, displays from A5 and A6, and a quick walkthrough of A3 and A4 with example lines. 3) Short live demo at the meat and bakery stands, plus a quick explanation from garden. If everyone is ok, I will finalize A7 and share the invite times.
From my side, that summary for T8 is good. The timing and content are clear.
Agreed, the plan for the mini-training works. I will make sure I can attend one of the sessions.
Ok for me as well. I will prepare the bakery example line in A4 before the training.
I am fine with the training plan and times. I will be ready to show the garden corner plan from A6 during the session.

For the end-of-campaign review in A8 and T12, I will schedule the 30-minute session for the week after the promotion ends and send a calendar invite. I will also prepare the A4 summary and a simple template in A8 where we can list successes, issues, and three improvement ideas. With that, we can say we are aligned on training time, attendees, and what will be included in the final review.
